transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: Public libraries across the United States are dramatically expanding their digital media collections, allowing patrons to borrow e-books, audiobooks, digital magazines, and even streaming movies and music from home. A new report from the American Library Association shows that digital checkouts have increased by over two hundred percent in the past five years, with many libraries now reporting that digital loans account for nearly half of all borrowing. To meet demand, libraries have increased their digital budgets by an average of thirty percent annually, negotiating with publishers to license more titles at lower costs. Some library systems have also started lending Wi-Fi hotspots and tablet computers to patrons who lack internet access or devices at home, helping bridge the digital divide. Library officials emphasize that digital services complement rather than replace physical books, as print circulation remains steady and libraries continue to serve as important community gathering spaces.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. How much have digital checkouts increased in the past five years?
2. What additional digital equipment are some libraries lending besides media?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: The city of Bristol is upgrading its recycling program to include weekly food waste collection, starting next month. The new service will allow residents to dispose of fruit and vegetable scraps, meat, fish, dairy products, and even small bones in specially provided brown bins, which will be collected weekly alongside regular recycling. The food waste will be taken to a local anaerobic digestion facility, where it will be converted into biogas to generate electricity and nutrient-rich fertilizer for farms. City officials estimate the program will divert over fifteen thousand tons of food waste from landfills each year, reducing methane emissions and producing enough electricity to power around two thousand homes. Residents will receive information packets and free kitchen caddies to help them separate food waste conveniently. The program is being introduced gradually across the city, with all neighborhoods covered by the end of the year.
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. What will happen to the collected food waste?
4. How many homes can be powered by the electricity produced?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology have developed a new type of solar panel that can convert over forty percent of sunlight into electricity, a significant improvement over the current average of around twenty to twenty-five percent for commercial panels. The breakthrough uses a multi-layer design that captures different wavelengths of light, combined with a special coating that reduces energy loss from heat. The team says the new panels can be manufactured using existing production lines, meaning they could be available to consumers within three to five years at a cost comparable to current high-efficiency panels. If widely adopted, the technology could dramatically reduce the cost of solar energy, making it more competitive with fossil fuels and accelerating the transition to renewable energy. The researchers are now working to improve durability, as the current prototypes degrade faster than traditional panels after prolonged exposure to the elements.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Rachel): Hey David, have you decided which electives to take next semester? I can't make up my mind.
Man (David): Hi Rachel, I'm still choosing too. We need to pick two electives, right? What subjects are you interested in?
Woman: I need something that fulfills the arts requirement, but I'm not very artistic. I was thinking about either art history or film studies.
Man: I took art history last year with Professor Henderson, and she's amazing. The class is really interesting even if you don't know much about art, and she makes the lectures really engaging.
Woman: How much work is it? I'm already taking some tough classes in my major, so I don't want an elective that requires tons of reading and papers.

Man: It's manageable. There's a textbook and some reading before each class, but the assignments are pretty straightforward - a midterm, a final, and one short paper about a work of art you choose yourself.
Woman: That doesn't sound too bad. What's film studies like? I watch a lot of movies, so that might be fun.

Man: I've heard film studies requires watching several movies a week and writing more papers - usually three or four over the semester. A friend of mine took it and said it's great but more time-consuming than you'd expect.
Woman: Hmm, maybe I'll go with art history then. What are you taking?

Man: I'm actually taking a creative writing class and a photography course. I've always wanted to improve my writing skills, and my sister gave me her old camera, so I thought I'd learn how to use it properly.
Woman: That sounds fun but creative writing sounds like a lot of work too.
Man: It probably will be, but I'm really looking forward to it. The professor is a published author, so I'm hoping to learn a lot. Have you considered any other electives?
Woman: I thought about music appreciation, but I don't know anything about music. Or public speaking - that might be useful for my future career.

Man: Public speaking is really practical. My roommate took it last semester and said it helped her feel much more confident giving presentations. But I heard you have to give several speeches in front of the class, which sounds terrifying to me.
Woman: That's exactly why I was considering it - I get really nervous speaking in front of people. But I'm also scared of the class itself.
Man: Sometimes the things that scare us are the most worthwhile.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
8. Which elective is the man considering for his arts requirement?
9. How many papers do students write for art history?
10. Why is the woman taking photography?
11. Why does the man consider public speaking?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Mike): Hey Sarah, I haven't seen you at the gym in a while. Did you give up on your fitness plan?
Woman (Sarah): No, Mike, I've just been really busy with work and classes. But I'm thinking about starting again. I just can't decide what kind of exercise to do.
Man: Well, what did you do before?
Woman: I used to run on the treadmill and lift weights, but I got bored with it after a couple of months. It felt like a chore rather than something enjoyable.
Man: That's a common problem. You need to find something you actually like doing, otherwise you won't stick with it. Have you tried any classes? The gym offers yoga, spinning, kickboxing, dance...
Woman: I tried yoga once, but I'm not very flexible and I felt silly because everyone else seemed to know what they were doing.
Man: Everyone feels that way at first! You get better with practice. What about swimming? It's great exercise and easy on your joints.
Woman: I actually like swimming. I used to swim on my high school team. But I don't like the gym pool - it's always crowded, and the chlorine really irritates my eyes.
Man: There's a community pool near campus that's supposed to be really nice and less crowded. Or maybe you could try something outdoorsy like hiking or cycling? The weather's been great lately.
Woman: I do enjoy hiking. There are some nice trails around the lake a few miles from campus. But I don't have a bike right now, and I need exercise I can do regularly, not just on weekends.

Man: What about joining a sports team? I'm on a recreational volleyball league. We play once a week, and it's really fun - you get exercise without even thinking about it because you're focused on the game.
Woman: That sounds interesting, but I haven't played volleyball in years. I'd probably be terrible.

Man: It's a recreational league - nobody's very good, and it's just for fun. We're always looking for more players. Or if team sports aren't your thing, there's a rock climbing gym that opened downtown recently. I've been wanting to try it.
Woman: Rock climbing does sound fun, but isn't it expensive?
Man: They have student discounts. Or you could come play volleyball with me next week - first game's free, so you can see if you like it.
Woman: That's really nice of you to offer. I think I'll take you up on that.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: For decades, parents were advised to keep pets away from babies and young children due to concerns that exposure to animal dander would increase the risk of developing allergies and asthma. However, a growing body of research suggests the opposite - that early exposure to pets, particularly dogs and cats, may actually reduce a child's risk of developing allergies later in life.

A major study following over five hundred children from birth to age seven found that those who lived with a dog during their first year of life were significantly less likely to develop allergies to pets, dust mites, and even common outdoor allergens like ragweed and grass. The "hygiene hypothesis" helps explain this phenomenon: our immune systems need exposure to microbes and allergens early in life to develop properly, learning to distinguish between harmful pathogens and harmless substances. Without this early exposure, the immune system may overreact to harmless particles, triggering allergic reactions.

The benefits appear strongest when exposure occurs during the first year of life, when the immune system is still developing. Children exposed to multiple pets or who grow up on farms around livestock have even lower rates of allergies. Researchers have also found that children in pet-owning households tend to have fewer sick days from school, fewer ear infections, and stronger immune systems overall, likely due to the diverse bacteria that pets bring into the home.

This doesn't mean every family should rush out to get a pet, especially if there's already a family history of severe allergies. But it does mean that parents shouldn't necessarily give up beloved family pets when a new baby arrives. The dirt and microbes that pets bring into the home might actually be one of the best early immune boosters a child can get.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Before email, text messaging, and social media, postcards were a popular and affordable way for people to communicate while traveling, send quick greetings to friends, and share images of faraway places. The golden age of postcards spanned from the late 1800s to the mid-1900s, a period when improved printing technology made mass production possible and postal services offered special low rates for postcard delivery.

The first commercially produced postcards appeared in the 1860s and 1870s, but they were plain cards with space for a message - no pictures. The picture postcard was introduced in the 1890s, and they quickly became a global phenomenon. People collected them in albums, sent them to friends and family, and purchased them as souvenirs when traveling. By 1905, Germany alone was producing over a billion postcards a year, and postcard collecting had become one of the most popular hobbies in Europe and North America.

Postcards provide a unique historical record of life in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. They document everything from street scenes and important events to fashion, architecture, and social customs, often showing details that professional photographers of the era ignored. Many postcards were hand-colored or artistically designed, making them miniature works of art as well as historical documents.

While postcards never regained their early 20th-century popularity after the telephone became widespread, they have experienced a small revival in recent years as people rediscover the joy of receiving physical mail in an increasingly digital world. Vintage postcards are also highly sought after by collectors, with rare examples selling for hundreds or even thousands of dollars at auction. Sending a postcard while traveling remains a simple, meaningful way to let someone know you're thinking of them.

20. Why are old postcards valuable to historians?

transcript.heading: Passage Three (British Female)
paras: Everyone has the same twenty-four hours in a day, yet some people seem to accomplish far more than others without feeling constantly stressed. The difference usually comes down to time management skills - but not the kind of rigid scheduling that makes life feel like a nonstop to-do list. Effective time management is about working smarter, not harder, and avoiding common pitfalls that waste time and energy.

One of the biggest mistakes people make is trying to multitask - doing several things at once, like answering emails while on a phone call or studying while watching television. Research consistently shows that multitasking actually reduces productivity and increases mistakes, because the brain can only focus deeply on one thing at a time. Instead, try "single-tasking" - devoting your full attention to one task for a set period before moving to the next.

Another common error is failing to prioritize tasks. Not everything on your to-do list is equally important, yet many people spend their day tackling small, easy tasks first because they provide a quick sense of accomplishment, while putting off larger, more important projects that would make a real difference. The "Eisenhower Matrix" helps solve this by categorizing tasks into four groups: urgent and important, important but not urgent, urgent but not important, and neither urgent nor important. Focus most of your energy on tasks that are important but not urgent - this is where planning, prevention, and long-term progress happen.

Procrastination is another major time waster, often caused by feeling overwhelmed by a large or unpleasant task. The solution is to break large tasks into small, manageable steps - instead of "write a paper," start with "spend ten minutes brainstorming topics." Also, don't underestimate the importance of rest and breaks. Working straight through without stopping actually decreases productivity and creativity over time. The Pomodoro Technique - working for twenty-five minutes then taking a five-minute break - is popular because it matches how our brains naturally function, alternating between focused attention and rest.
